In this surah the separation is applied to opponents and their money; in the other it is applied to the believing community itself. The wording of the phrase is identical in both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assigns a use to something intended as opposition. Money raised to stop a message is described as serving a sorting that nobody involved was aiming at. That is a strong claim about how history runs, and the Quran makes it repeatedly: hostile action is not outside the account but inside it. The closing word keeps the register commercial, so the verdict arrives as a balance rather than a sentence.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about separating foul from good, applied there to the community itself.
Describes the spending that this ayah then assigns a purpose to, in the line immediately before.
Uses the same verb for heaping, there of clouds stacking together before the rain falls.

studies.applyIt: Notice something currently working against you, and ask what it is separating rather than what it is costing. It may be showing you which of your commitments are load-bearing and which were decorative. Write down one of each. Do not act on it yet. The ayah is about seeing the sorting, not about redesigning your life this week.

studies.title: What Is Past Will Be Forgiven
studies.meaning: An offer made through an intermediary, and its terms are unusually plain. Stopping is the only condition named, and what is offered in return is the whole of the past. No penance is required, no restitution mentioned, no apology asked for. The alternative arrives not as a threat but as a precedent: a pattern has already run in earlier cases and its course is known. That leaves the decision with the hearer and takes the drama out of the warning.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to the Meccan opposition in the period after Badr. The commentators read the offer as a genuine one rather than rhetorical, and note that within a few years many of those addressed did stop and were treated exactly as the ayah describes. The word for what has passed covers everything up to the moment of stopping, which the commentators emphasise when they discuss how far the offer reaches.

keyTerms.note: The verb for reaching a limit and going no further. It asks for cessation, not for repair or apology, which is why the offer can be stated without any further conditions hanging off it.
A word for what has preceded, used of ancestors and of money paid in advance. Applied to deeds, it treats the past as a completed transaction that can be written off in full.
The word for a track worn into ground by repeated passage. Applied to earlier peoples it names a course already run rather than a rule imposed, so the warning takes the form of a precedent.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia ended by settlement, never by forgetting. Blood money was counted out, camels handed over, and the arrangement recited publicly so everyone knew the account was closed. An offer to cancel a past without any payment would have sounded extraordinary to people whose entire system for ending a conflict was built on precise and witnessed compensation.
studies.didYouKnow: The same offer appears twice in this surah, at 8:19 and here, nineteen ayat apart, both times addressed to the same audience and using the same pair of verbs for stopping and for returning. In both places the offer is stated before the warning rather than after it, which reverses the order these two usually take.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes forgiveness available at the point of stopping rather than at the point of atoning. That sets the threshold very low and the offer very wide, and it is extended towards people who had just fought a battle against the community. It also treats history as evidence: what follows a refusal is pointed at rather than asserted, which invites a reader to go and check rather than simply to be frightened.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same offer to the same audience, in the same conditional form, nineteen ayat earlier.
States the same width of forgiveness with no conditions of restitution attached to it.
Applies the same principle to grave wrongs, where stopping in time changes what follows.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose stopping you would not accept, because of what they did before they stopped. You are not obliged to trust them again. But notice the distance between what this ayah offers and what you are offering, and ask whether that distance is protecting you or only costing you. One sentence of acknowledgement often covers all of it.

studies.title: The Best Of Protectors
studies.meaning: An instruction given to a community already at war, with its own end condition written into it. Two things mark the point at which it stops: the ending of persecution, and religion belonging wholly to God. Commentators differ over the scope of the second phrase, some reading it as the removal of coercion and others more widely. The next sentence makes stopping the operative condition again, and the passage closes not on victory but on two names describing God as protector and helper.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the period after Badr when open conflict with Mecca was under way and the community was organising for it. The word rendered as persecution had a concrete referent for the first listeners: believers still in Mecca who could not practise openly and could not leave. The commentators read the instruction against that background, and the surah has already reported the same conflict from several angles.

keyTerms.note: The same word used a few ayat earlier of wealth and children as a test. Here the commentators read it in its harder sense, of pressure applied to make somebody abandon what they hold.

The verb for reaching a limit and going no further, used three times in this surah of the same audience. Each time it appears the sentence around it changes direction, which makes stopping the hinge of the argument.
From a root meaning nearness. In Arabian usage it named the relationship of protection between a clan and someone attached to it, so the closing line answers the question of who will stand for you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection was the fundamental social fact of Arabia. Without a patron a person had no standing, no recourse and no safety on the roads. Freed slaves and outsiders sought that attachment explicitly, and the word for it was in daily use. Ending a passage about conflict by naming God with that word placed the community inside a relationship its listeners understood exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The word closing this passage belongs to a small class of Arabic words that name both sides of a relationship at once: patron and client, protector and protected, master and freed man. Which sense applies is decided entirely by the surrounding words, and here the two phrases that follow settle it beyond any doubt.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is given with a stopping point attached, and that stopping point is stated twice. The structure matters more than any single clause, since what is described is bounded by a condition rather than left open. The closing turn is worth noticing too. After several ayat about force, the passage ends by naming a relationship, and the reassurance offered is not that you will win but that you are held.

crossReferences.why: States the same instruction with the same stopping condition, and adds where hostility ends.
Gives the corresponding instruction if the other side inclines to peace, later in this surah.
Ends with the identical pair of phrases naming God as protector and as helper.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often a conflict of yours has no stated end condition. Not a war, just a running argument with a relative or a colleague. Write down in one sentence what would have to be true for it to be over. If you cannot write it, that itself is the finding. This passage attaches a stopping point to the hardest instruction it gives.

studies.title: The Day Of Distinction
studies.meaning: A distribution is set out, and its most striking feature is who gets named in it. After God and the Messenger come relatives, orphans, the poor, and the traveller left without resources, so three of the four human categories are categories of need. The passage then attaches the whole arrangement to belief and dates it, to what was sent down on the day the two groups met. Commentators discuss the details at length; the ayah itself turns a question about ownership into a list of people.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the encounter at Badr and answering the dispute this surah opened with. The commentators report that the ayah settled the question raised at 8:1 by naming a structure rather than adjudicating between claimants. The day is given a title here, the day of distinction, which the classical sources treat as a name for that battle, and the phrase occurs nowhere else in the Quran.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers acquiring something at no cost as well as taking it in war, and the same root gives the ordinary Arabic word for sheep. What it names is a gain that arrives rather than a wage that is earned.
The plain fraction. Naming a proportion rather than a sum means the arrangement scales with whatever is gained, and it leaves the larger part unaddressed here, which is what the commentators discuss.
From the root meaning to separate. The Quran uses this word for revelation itself and for the faculty of telling right from wrong, so naming a day with it makes the day an instrument of separation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dividing what a raiding party took was governed by custom that varied between tribes and produced constant argument. A leader customarily took a quarter off the top for himself before anything at all was shared out. Setting aside a fifth instead, and directing much of it towards orphans, the poor and stranded travellers, changed both the fraction and the direction in which it flowed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming that day, the day of distinction, occurs only here in the Quran. The word inside it is used elsewhere for revelation itself, and it titles surah 25. Applying it to a day rather than to a book happens in this ayah alone, and the classical commentators take it as a name for the encounter at Badr.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage converts a dispute over property into an ordered relation. Assigning a portion upward and then downward through categories of need means that settling a quarrel is simultaneously a provision for people who were never party to it. And attaching the whole arrangement to belief, inside a conditional clause, treats a question about goods as continuous with the question of what the community actually is.

crossReferences.why: Records the dispute this ayah answers, at the very opening of the same surah.
States the principle behind directing wealth downward, in a later and closely related passage.
Names almost the same four categories of recipient inside a description of righteousness.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you decide what to do with money that arrives unexpectedly: a refund, a gift, a bonus. Most people fold it into ordinary spending within a week. Before the next one comes, decide the fraction and the direction in advance, and name one person or place it goes to. Deciding beforehand is what this ayah makes possible.

studies.title: Upon A Clear Evidence
studies.meaning: The geography comes first, stated flatly: one force on the near slope, one on the far one, the caravan passing below and out of reach. Then the passage says the encounter could not have been arranged, since any agreed meeting would have collapsed in the planning of it. What stands in place of an arrangement is a matter already settled. And the purpose given is not victory but clarity, so that whoever went down and whoever came through did so with the question no longer open.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, recalling the ground at Badr. The wells lay in a valley with rising land on either side, and the caravan the expedition had set out to intercept passed along the coast below and got away. Neither force had chosen the site in advance. The commentators dwell on the improbability of the meeting and read the ayah as removing it from the category of things anybody present had planned.

keyTerms.note: The raised edge of a watercourse. Naming both sides with one word, the nearer and the further, gives the scene its symmetry and quietly places the speaker with one of the two forces.
A reciprocal form: a promise made by two parties to each other. The Arabic requires both sides to have agreed, which is what makes the sentence about disagreement so pointed.
From a root meaning to become distinct. It names whatever separates itself from its surroundings, so the phrase describes going down or surviving with the situation no longer ambiguous.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arranging a meeting across desert was genuinely difficult. Water sources fixed the possible routes, and a day's error in either direction meant missing each other entirely. Tribes negotiating a truce sent messengers back and forth for weeks over the place and the date. The counterfactual in this ayah would have landed on its first listeners as an obvious fact rather than a rhetorical flourish.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the side of a valley occurs only in this ayah, where it is used twice, once for each slope. The Quran gives the position of both forces and of the caravan in a single line, which is the closest thing to a map anywhere in it, and then spends the rest of the ayah saying that none of the arrangement was human.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage supplies a reason for an event, and the reason is not about winning. What the encounter produced, on this account, is a situation in which nothing further could be claimed to be unclear. That makes clarity a purpose worth an event, which is a strong claim to make. It also lifts both credit and blame for the meeting away from everyone involved, without denying that they fought it.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same account, describing how each side was made to see the other.
Describes what the men had wanted instead, and why the caravan was the preferred object.
Shows the same kind of after-the-fact reasoning about a battle nobody had planned for.

studies.applyIt: Think of a meeting or a coincidence that changed something for you and that nobody arranged. Trace it back three steps and notice how many small things had to go wrong for it to happen at all. The ayah is not asking you to feel grateful. It is asking you to be accurate about how little of it was scheduled.

studies.title: Shown To You As Few
studies.meaning: A perception is described as having been adjusted, and then the alternative outcome is stated without softening: losing heart, and falling into argument about what to do. Those are the two ways a small force comes apart, and the passage names them in that order. What is claimed is not that the numbers were different but that what was seen was. The closing clause credits the whole thing to God rather than to the man who saw it, and ends by naming knowledge of what is inside chests.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the night before the fighting at Badr. The classical sources treat the dream as a true dream given to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and the commentators discuss whether the fewness shown concerned the opposing force's number or its resolve. They record both readings without settling between them. The ayah belongs to a stretch that returns to the same day repeatedly from different angles.

keyTerms.note: The word names the state rather than the vision, so the Arabic says He showed them to you in your sleeping. The Quran uses the same word elsewhere for sleep as a sign and for souls taken at night.
The verb for nerve failing, distinct from being afraid and from fleeing. It names resolve draining away while a person still stands where they were, which is why it precedes the dispute.

From the root for wholeness and peace. The verb here is given no object at all, which commentators note: what was preserved is left unnamed, so a reader supplies the men, the outcome, or the whole situation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Estimating an opposing force was guesswork done from dust clouds, campfires and the size of a camp. Scouts brought back impressions rather than figures, and those impressions decided whether men would fight at all. In a society with no maps and no standing armies, what a force believed about the other side's size was often the single most important fact of the day.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical accounts of the days before this encounter describe scouts estimating the opposing force by counting how many camels were being slaughtered to feed it each day. The Quran reports none of that. It reports a dream instead, and then spends the ayah on what the dream did to the men who were told about it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes perception itself an arena of divine action. That is a delicate claim, and the passage keeps it honest by naming the alternative rather than simply asserting a benefit: without the adjustment, the force would have come apart before contact. It also identifies argument as the second stage of losing nerve, which is a precise observation about how groups fail when they are frightened.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same adjustment happening again at the moment the two forces actually met.
Names dispute as the thing that dissolves a group, which this ayah lists as the second failure.
Shows a true dream treated as reliable information across many years, in another prophet's account.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your courage this week rested on an estimate rather than on a fact: the size of the task, the number of people who disagree, how long it will take. Write down one such estimate and where it came from. Most of them turn out to have no source at all, which is worth knowing before you act.

studies.title: Stand Firm And Remember
studies.meaning: The adjustment described a line earlier is now shown running in both directions at once. Each side was made to see the other as smaller than it was, which is not a straightforward advantage to either of them. Commentators explain it as bringing on an engagement that both might otherwise have avoided. Then the address turns to the believers, and what is asked for on meeting a force is a pair of things: stand still, and remember God a great deal. Nothing at all is said about tactics.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the account of Badr. The commentators note that the two-way diminishing worked to bring about the meeting rather than to favour one party, and connect it to the phrase in the previous ayah about a matter already decided. The instruction in the second ayah is general in form, and the surah has already given a related one about not turning away from an advancing line.

keyTerms.gloss: and He makes you appear few
keyTerms.note: A causative of the verb for being few. Applied to how one side looked in the other's eyes, it describes an adjustment of what was seen rather than any change in the number of men present.

From the same root used earlier in this surah of the angels steadying believers. Here the instruction is turned round and given to the men themselves, so what was received in one ayah is asked for in another.
From a root meaning to split open, used of a farmer breaking ground. Success in Arabic is pictured as cutting through to what lies underneath rather than as arriving somewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The remembering asked for here had a recognisable rival. Men going into a fight in Arabia chanted, called out their lineage and shouted the names of their clan, both to hold their nerve and to identify one another in a press of bodies. Replacing that with the remembrance of God was not adding a devotion to the day. It was substituting one thing for another at a precise moment.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind standing firm runs through this surah's battle account four times, applied in turn to feet steadied on wet ground at 8:11, to what the angels were told to do at 8:12, to a plot in Mecca to hold a man in place at 8:30, and finally here to the men themselves. One image of fixing something covers help, hostility and instruction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is asked for at the hardest moment is remembrance rather than exertion. That is unexpected in a passage about a battle, and it is not decorative: standing still and turning attention elsewhere are both given as things to do in the middle of an engagement. It implies that what a person attends to under pressure is itself an action, and one with consequences the passage is willing to name.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root for making firm, applied there to feet on wet ground and to the angels.
Records the same request made by an earlier outnumbered force before an engagement began.
Gives the same instruction to remember much, in a setting with no danger in it at all.

studies.applyIt: Pick the moment in your week when you are most likely to react badly: a particular meeting, a particular hour with the children, the journey home. Attach one short phrase of remembrance to it in advance. Not as a charm, but so that your attention has somewhere to go at the moment it would otherwise scatter.

studies.title: Your Wind Will Go
studies.meaning: Three instructions with a consequence set between them. Obey, do not quarrel with one another, and be steadfast, and the middle one carries the weight: internal dispute is said to produce two effects, losing heart and losing your wind. The commentators explain the second as the force that carries a group forward, and the image is meteorological rather than martial. The closing clause names what steadfastness gets, and it is company rather than victory.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the section of the surah giving instruction for confrontation, after the account of Badr. Disagreements over strategy and over the division of gains had already appeared, and the surah opens with one of them. The commentators read this ayah as addressing that pattern directly rather than as general advice, and the warning against disputing comes before the call to endure.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form of the verb to snatch or pull. The image is of two parties tugging the same thing in opposite directions, which is why the result described is a loss of forward movement.
A verb for weakness arising from within rather than from an opponent. It names failure of nerve specifically, and it is placed as the immediate result of the quarrel rather than of anything external.
The ordinary word for wind, used of a group's force and standing. Commentators explain it as the impetus that carries people along, and a becalmed vessel is the picture behind it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab forces were coalitions of clans, each with its own leader, its own honour to protect and its own view of when to fight. Armies dissolved when one contingent withdrew, and a public argument between leaders could empty a field before anything began. Everyone hearing this had watched a gathering come apart that way. The warning described the ordinary cause of defeat, not an exotic one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the momentum a community loses is the everyday word for wind, and the Quran uses the same word elsewhere for the winds that carry rain and for the gale that destroyed an earlier people. Choosing it here makes a group's cohesion something like weather: real, forceful, and impossible to hold once it has turned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Internal disagreement is treated as a material cause with material effects, not as a moral failing to be regretted afterwards. The sequence is precise: quarrelling produces loss of nerve, and loss of nerve produces loss of force. Steadfastness is then named as the remedy, and what it earns is stated as company rather than as an outcome, which is a smaller promise than victory and a considerably more reliable one.

crossReferences.why: Commands holding to the same rope together and recalls the hearts that were joined.
Traces a reverse at Uhud to failure of nerve and dispute over an order.
Uses the same closing formula, that God is with those who are patient.

studies.applyIt: In the next group you are part of that is stuck, resist the urge to win the argument for one more meeting and instead ask what everyone actually agrees on. Say that list out loud. The ayah treats disagreement as something that drains a shared force, and naming the common ground is the cheapest way to stop the draining.

studies.title: Out Of Their Homes Boasting
studies.meaning: An instruction delivered entirely as a negative example. Three things are named about the other side's departure, and the first two concern an audience rather than an aim: swagger, and being seen by people. Only the third names a purpose. Commentators note that the word for boasting describes a person made unsteady by good fortune, so what is pictured is not courage but a kind of intoxication. The closing clause says all of it is encompassed, which answers the wish to be seen without argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect the ayah to reports of the Meccan force setting out for Badr with a public display of confidence, some recording that a proposal to turn back once the caravan was safe was overruled in favour of making an appearance. The reports differ in detail and agree on the general picture. The ayah uses that episode as a warning to the community rather than as narrative.

keyTerms.note: A word for the state of somebody unbalanced by good fortune, close to being spoiled by ease. It names an attitude towards blessings rather than towards other people, and occurs only here.

keyTerms.gloss: and to be seen, for show
keyTerms.note: From the verb to see, in a form meaning to make oneself seen. The Quran uses it for acts done with an audience in mind, and it became the standard term for hollow display in religion.
The participle of a verb meaning to surround completely, used of a wall enclosing a garden. Applied to God's awareness it answers a wish to be seen with the fact of being seen entirely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A departure was a performance in Arabia. A force leaving a town went out in full view, with poets composing on the spot and women watching from the roofs, and the manner of the leaving was reported afterwards alongside the result. Coming home quietly from an abandoned expedition cost real standing. That pressure explains a great deal about why forces met at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for boastful pride here occurs only in this ayah, and the verb it comes from appears once more at 28:58, describing a whole town that had grown insolent in its way of living. The word for acting to be seen occurs three times, all of them in Medinan surahs and all attached to something being done in public.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage warns a community about a manner rather than an action. Both sides marched out; what is set out of bounds here is marching out with an audience in view. That makes intention a genuine object of instruction rather than a private matter beyond reach. And the name chosen for God at the close is exact: to someone acting for spectators, an awareness that surrounds everything is the precise answer.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same expedition from the side of what it cost, and where the money went.
Applies the same word for display to charity, and describes what it does to a good deed.
Names the same fault inside an act of worship that is outwardly entirely correct.

studies.applyIt: Before you next post, mention or otherwise report something good you have done, wait an hour. Not to suppress it; there is nothing wrong with people knowing. Just notice, during that hour, how much of the impulse survives once the audience is delayed. That gap is the whole of what this ayah describes.

studies.title: I See What You Do Not
studies.meaning: A promise and its withdrawal, set on either side of a single moment. The encouragement is offered in the language of protection, using a word that carried real obligations in Arabia, and it holds exactly until the two forces come into sight of each other. Then three sentences of retraction arrive, each opening the same way. Commentators handle the last of them carefully: the claim to fear God is reported without comment, and they differ over how to read it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the Meccan force before Badr. The classical sources connect the ayah to reports of assurances given to the Meccans before they set out, and the commentators record more than one account of the form the encouragement took. They agree about what the passage is doing: describing a confidence supplied from outside and withdrawn at the exact moment it would have cost something to keep.

keyTerms.note: The verb for decorating or adorning. It changes nothing about what is decorated, only how it appears, which is why the Quran uses it for the presentation of actions rather than for their nature.

In Arabian usage a neighbour was someone under your protection and owed yours, a formal relation with real cost attached. Claiming it meant claiming to be answerable, which is what makes the withdrawal a breach.

keyTerms.gloss: he turned back on his heels
keyTerms.note: A verb for retreating backwards without turning round, so the face stays towards what is being abandoned. It appears only twice in the Quran, and describes a movement rather than a decision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection between neighbours was among the strongest bonds in Arabia and did not depend on kinship at all. A man could grant it to a stranger, and having granted it he was expected to fight for that person. Breaking it was one of the most shameful things that could be said of anyone. That is the relationship being claimed here, and it was dropped at the first cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives this disavowal twice. Here it happens on a battlefield as the two forces come into view; at 14:22 the same figure makes a longer version of it after the reckoning, telling his followers that he had no authority over them and did nothing but call, while they answered. The two speeches make the same argument at opposite ends of time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes how false confidence works, and the description is structural rather than moral. Something makes an action look good; a promise of security is attached to it; the promise holds until it is tested; then the guarantor withdraws and the person who acted is left holding the action alone. That sequence needs no enemy in it. It is how a bad decision usually feels from the inside.

crossReferences.why: Records the same withdrawal after the reckoning, in a speech that explains its own terms.
Gives the same pattern as a short parable, with the same words of disavowal at the end.
Describes the same expedition and the same confidence, from the side of what was spent.

studies.applyIt: Think about where your confidence for a large decision actually came from. Often it was a person who will not be there when it goes wrong, and who was never asked to be. Name the source out loud before you commit next time. Not to become fearful, but so you know which parts of your assurance are load-bearing.

studies.title: Deluded By Their Religion
studies.meaning: An accusation is quoted and then not answered. The charge is that faith had made a small force overestimate itself, which is exactly what an outside observer would have concluded from the numbers alone. The passage does not dispute the arithmetic. It changes the subject to the relation involved, naming reliance on God, and then closes with two names instead of a result. Commentators note that the reply defines what reliance is rather than promising what it will produce.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing observers at the time of Badr. The commentators identify the speakers in more than one way, some reading them as people in Medina who had not gone out and others as men who had come with the Meccan force. The ayah names two groups separately, which the commentators discuss, and they generally treat sickness of heart as a condition rather than as membership of a party.

keyTerms.gloss: it deluded, it took them in
keyTerms.note: The verb for deceiving somebody with an appearance. The same root gives the Arabic word for a person too inexperienced to see a danger, so the charge being made is of naivety rather than of dishonesty.

The ordinary word for illness. The Quran applies it to hearts as a settled condition that grows, distinct from ordinary doubt, and the phrase names people by their state rather than by any allegiance.
From a root meaning to appoint somebody as your agent. Reliance in Arabic is not passivity but delegation: handing a matter over to someone able to act, once you have done what you can with it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The numbers at Badr were public knowledge and the arithmetic was not subtle. A few hundred lightly equipped men against a force perhaps three times their size, with horses and supplies behind it. Any experienced person in Medina could work out the likely result on their fingers. The accusation quoted here was not malice inventing a story. It was the sensible reading of the situation.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a sickness in the heart occurs eleven times in the Quran and is used mainly of people inside the community rather than of opponents outside it. That is what makes it an uncomfortable phrase to read. It names a condition that can develop in someone already counted among the believers, and it is described as growing rather than as fixed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply does not defend the believers or claim they had calculated correctly. It shifts the ground: what looked from outside like a miscalculation is described from inside as a relation. That does not make the criticism wrong on its own terms, and the passage never says it does. It says the terms are not the only ones available, and it declines to offer an outcome as proof.

crossReferences.why: Records the same situation from inside, where a report of larger numbers increased faith instead.
States the same relation as a general principle, with the promise this ayah withholds.
Answers the arithmetic directly, in the account of an earlier outnumbered company.

studies.applyIt: Someone has told you a commitment of yours is unrealistic, and they may well be right about the numbers. Do not argue the numbers. Ask yourself separately what you are actually relying on, and whether you have done your own part of the work first. Reliance in this ayah is delegation after effort, not instead of it.

studies.title: What Your Hands Sent Forward
studies.meaning: A scene the reader is invited to see, opening with a conditional that is never completed: if only you could see. What follows describes a departure rather than a punishment proper, angels at the moment of death, and the speech attributed to them is very short. The second ayah then gives the reason in one clause and closes with a denial about God, phrased in a form that rules out even the smallest measure of injustice.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's account of the aftermath of Badr, where a number of the Meccan leadership were killed. The commentators read the passage as describing what happens at death generally rather than as a report about named individuals, and note that it moves from the third person into direct address partway through. The ayat that follow place the whole scene inside a much older pattern.

keyTerms.note: The verb for collecting a debt or a payment completely, with nothing left owing. The Quran uses it for death, so dying is described as a settlement taken in full rather than as an ending.
An intensive form naming fire by what it does rather than by what it is. Arabic distinguishes it from the ordinary word for a fire, and the Quran uses it in only a handful of places.
The verb for sending something on ahead of you, as a traveller sends baggage to the next halt. It makes deeds arrive before the person does, waiting at the destination rather than trailing behind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans sent goods, and sometimes people, ahead to the next stopping place so that arrangements were made before the main party arrived. Everyone who travelled understood the arrangement and its risk: whatever you sent ahead was what would be waiting when you got there, and nothing about it could be altered on the road. The ayah's verb for deeds comes out of that practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence that closes this passage occurs word for word at 3:182 and, with one small alteration, at 22:10. The phrase denying that God wrongs His servants stands at the very end of an ayah every time it appears in the Quran, five times in all. It is never a claim a sentence opens with; it always arrives as the last word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the reason and the reassurance inside the same sentence. What is happening is attributed to what the person did, and then the possibility that God has been unjust is denied in the same breath, using a grammatical form that excludes even a small measure. Placing those together means the description is not asking a reader to accept a hard scene on trust. It offers an account of it.

crossReferences.why: Ends with exactly the same sentence, in a passage about words spoken rather than a battle.
Describes the same moment of death with the same figures present, in a Meccan passage.
Continues immediately, setting the whole scene inside a much older repeated pattern.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you sent ahead today. Not the large questions; the actual content of the hours. A message you did not send, a person you were short with, ten minutes given to someone who needed them. The image in this ayah is baggage waiting at the next halt. Add one thing to it before you sleep.

studies.title: The Same Habit Again
studies.meaning: A comparison is made and its terms are exact. The word used is not for a single act but for a customary way of going about things, so what is matched is a habit rather than an event. Two groups are named, one specific and one left open, and the offence given is the denial of signs. The consequence arrives through a verb of seizing, which is physical, and it is attributed to their own wrongdoing. The whole ayah returns in altered form two lines later.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the description of what happened to those killed at Badr. The commentators read the comparison as the surah's way of placing a recent event inside a long series, and note that the same opening phrase occurs twice within three ayat, each time with a different verb after it. The phrase appears once more in the Quran, in a passage of surah 3 that also concerns a battle.

keyTerms.note: The word means a settled custom, the way somebody habitually goes about things, and it also carries a sense of persistent effort. It compares conduct sustained over time rather than any single incident.
The plain verb for taking hold of something. The Quran uses it of consequences arriving, and its bluntness is the point: no process is described at all, only a grip closing.
The second word comes from the root for a heel, so what follows wrongdoing is named as the thing that comes along behind it. Arabic builds the idea of consequence out of that image.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: History in Arabia was carried as a stock of examples rather than as a chronology. Ruined settlements along the trade routes were pointed out to travellers, and the story attached to each was told as a pattern rather than as a dated event. Comparing a recent defeat to the people of Pharaoh would have registered as ordinary reasoning, not as a rhetorical reach.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening phrase of this ayah occurs three times in the Quran: twice in this surah, here and again at 8:54, and once at 3:11. All three sit inside a passage about a battle, and each time it introduces a comparison to a much older people rather than to any recent opponent. Nothing else in the surah is repeated so closely at such short range.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comparison does something specific to the recent event: it removes its uniqueness. What happened at Badr is presented as one instance of a thing with a long record behind it, which discourages the side that won from reading it as a statement about themselves. Naming the offence as denial of signs, rather than as opposition to a community, also keeps the account from becoming tribal.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same opening phrase two ayat later, with stronger verbs and a named ending.
Uses the identical phrase in the account of a different battle, with the same comparison.
Places a warning inside the same kind of list, spoken by a man of Pharaoh's own household.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you treat something that happened to you as unprecedented. Bad weeks feel singular, and they almost never are. Ask one person who has been where you are what the pattern usually looks like. The relief in this ayah is not that the pattern is pleasant. It is that there is one, and it can be learned.

studies.title: Until They Change Themselves
studies.meaning: The principle appears here in a specific form that is easy to miss. What is said not to change is a blessing already granted, and the condition attached concerns what is inside the people holding it. Read closely, this is a statement about loss rather than about improvement: it explains why something given is withdrawn. Commentators note the difference from the better known version of the principle elsewhere, which speaks of a people's whole condition rather than of a favour they already have.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, given as the explanation of the comparison just drawn to older peoples. The commentators treat the ayah as stating the rule behind the entire sequence of ruined communities the surah has been invoking. They read the blessing broadly, covering security, provision and standing together, and note that it addresses a community which had itself just received a considerable one.

keyTerms.note: A participle rather than a verb, placed under a negation of the whole state. The Arabic says God is not one who changes, which describes a manner of acting rather than a single decision taken once.
An indefinite noun, so any blessing at all rather than one in particular. Its root also gives the words for softness and ease, so what is named is comfort supplied rather than status conferred.

The plural of the word for a soul or a self. The condition is located inside people rather than in their circumstances, which is what separates this statement from an ordinary account of cause and effect.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prosperity in Arabia was visibly fragile. A well could silt up, a trade route could shift to a rival town, an alliance could lapse and a settlement decline inside a generation. Ruined places along the roads made the point without anyone needing to argue it. What people disputed was the cause, and the usual explanations reached for fate, luck or a broken oath rather than anything internal.
studies.didYouKnow: This principle occurs twice in the Quran in closely matched wording, here and at 13:11. The two differ in what is said to change. In this ayah it is a blessing already given; in the other it is a people's condition as a whole. Commentators read the pair together, and it is one of the closest verbal parallels between two distant surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The rule cuts more sharply in one direction than the other. It explains why blessings are withdrawn, and locates the cause inside the people who held them rather than in a decision taken about them from outside. That makes loss intelligible without making it arbitrary. It also implies something demanding: a community's outward condition is treated as an expression of its inward one, over time rather than immediately.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle with a wider subject, a people's condition rather than one blessing.
Names the pattern this ayah explains, in the line immediately before it.
Gives the other direction of the same relation, between an inward state and what follows from it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something good in your life that has quietly deteriorated: a friendship, a skill, a habit of prayer. Resist the explanation involving other people or circumstances, just for five minutes. Ask what changed in you first. The ayah is not accusing you. It is telling you where to look, which is usually the harder half.

studies.title: And We Drowned Them
studies.meaning: The same comparison is made again two ayat later, and almost everything in it has shifted. The verb for denial takes a stronger form, seizing becomes destruction, the speaker moves from the third person into the first, and one specific ending is named rather than left general. Commentators note the pairing and read the second as the completed version of the first. The closing clause then spreads the verdict across everyone mentioned rather than confining it to the ruler.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The account of Moses and Pharaoh is the Quran's most frequently told narrative, and this ayah invokes only its ending. The commentators note that a Medinan audience would have known the story in detail, from the surrounding communities as well as from earlier revelation. What is used here is not the story but its conclusion, placed last in a list of precedents.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, stronger than the verb used of the same people two ayat earlier. The escalation between the two versions is deliberate, since the second telling raises every element of the first.

The verb for bringing something to ruin. The shift into the first person plural here, after a third person account two ayat before, is what commentators point to as the difference between the tellings.
From a root meaning darkness and, by extension, putting something where it does not belong. The word covers wrong done to others and to oneself, and the ayah applies it to everybody just mentioned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drowning was a strange death to invoke in a desert country, and that is part of its force. Arabs knew the sea from the Red Sea trade and from the crossing to Abyssinia, and wrecks along the coast were a real hazard. A whole force lost to water was an image of complete disappearance: no bodies to bury, no field to mark, nothing left to point at afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: Moses is named more often in the Quran than any other figure, and the end of Pharaoh's people is told in many surahs at many different lengths. This ayah gives it in a few words. The Quran regularly compresses a narrative it has told at length elsewhere into a single clause, whenever the point being made is the pattern rather than the story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repeating a comparison with every element intensified makes a claim about seriousness rather than adding information. The second version names an ending, and the ending is total. But the closing clause does something further: it says all of them were wrongdoers, which spreads responsibility from a ruler to the people who went along with him. That refusal to let a people shelter behind a leader recurs throughout the Quran.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first and milder version of this comparison, two ayat earlier in the same passage.
Narrates the ending this ayah compresses, including what was said at the last moment.
Explains how responsibility spread from the ruler to the people who obeyed him.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you explain a group's behaviour by naming its leader. It is usually accurate and usually incomplete. Pick one situation where you have done that this month and ask what the people around the leader were doing. Then ask the same question about a group you belong to yourself.

studies.title: Broken Every Single Time
studies.meaning: The verdict from earlier in the surah returns with a different description attached, and the description now concerns agreements rather than understanding. What is named is not one breach but a pattern: broken every time. The third ayah then addresses a specific wartime situation, and its stated purpose is the deterrence of others rather than the punishment of those present. Commentators discuss how far the instruction reaches and tie it closely to the treaty-breaking just described.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Agreements between the community in Medina and groups in and around the city were formal arrangements with named terms, and this passage addresses a situation in which some had been broken more than once. The commentators identify particular parties and differ about them. What the reports agree on is the pattern the ayat name: agreements entered into and then set aside repeatedly.

keyTerms.note: The verb for undoing something twisted, used of unpicking a rope back into its separate fibres. It pictures an agreement as a braided thing, so breaking it is taking it apart rather than merely ignoring it.
The word for a covenant, used equally of a treaty between peoples and of the pledge given to God. Arabic does not separate the two registers, which is why one word carries both weights in this surah.

The verb for driving something away so that it does not settle again. The stated aim is those behind them rather than those in front, so the instruction is framed as prevention rather than as a penalty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A treaty in Arabia was spoken, witnessed and remembered, with no document anyone could consult afterwards. Its force came entirely from what breaking it would cost you in standing among people who would hear about it. A party willing to bear that cost repeatedly was effectively outside the system, since nothing else existed to hold them. That is the situation these ayat describe.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the worst of creatures occurs only twice in the Quran, and both occurrences are in this surah, at 8:22 and here at 8:55. The wording is identical up to the point where the description begins. The first names people who will not use their minds; the second names people who will not keep their word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats the keeping of agreements as a matter of the highest seriousness, applying to it the same phrase used earlier of the refusal to think. That puts reliability among the fundamentals rather than among the courtesies. And by locating the fault in repetition rather than in a single failure, it leaves room for the ordinary breaking and mending of arrangements that any society lives by.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for the worst of creatures, with a different description attached.
Gives the corresponding instruction when treachery is only feared rather than established.
Uses the same image of unravelling for oath-breaking, and gives it a memorable comparison.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small commitment you make and break regularly: a time you say you will arrive, a call you say you will return. Nobody treats it as serious, including you. Pick that one and keep it exactly for two weeks. The passage is about repetition, and repetition is the only thing that can answer it.

studies.title: Throw It Back Openly
studies.meaning: A rule of procedure whose whole content is notice. If treachery is feared rather than proven, what is called for is returning the agreement openly, on equal terms, so that both parties know where they stand. The phrase about equal terms carries the weight: nothing may be taken from the other side's ignorance. Commentators read the closing clause as covering whoever acts first quite as much as whoever breaks faith. The following ayah then answers a different worry.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the description of agreements broken repeatedly. The commentators read this ayah as governing the community's own conduct rather than its opponents', and note that it addresses the moment before anything has actually happened: suspicion, not proof. The setting was a city of overlapping arrangements where information was partial and rumour moved faster than confirmation ever could.

keyTerms.note: The same root used earlier in the surah for betraying a trust. Here it names something feared rather than established, which is why the instruction concerns notice rather than reprisal.

The verb for tossing something aside, used elsewhere in the Quran of scripture cast behind the back. Here the same physical image is put to a legitimate use: returning an agreement rather than discarding a duty.
From a root meaning evenness. The phrase requires the other party to be left in the same position of knowledge as you, so no advantage can be taken from the interval before they find out.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a world without written contracts, the moment an agreement ended mattered enormously. A party that considered itself free while the other still thought itself bound could act with total surprise, and that was the ordinary way raids succeeded. Requiring a public return of the agreement removed exactly that advantage, and removed it from the side being addressed rather than from anyone else.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for returning an agreement is the same one used at 3:187 of people who threw the scripture behind their backs. The Quran puts one physical image to work in two directions: once for an obligation discarded, and once for an obligation formally handed back. Only the object and the manner separate the two uses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction constrains the party holding the advantage. Someone who suspects treachery has every practical reason to strike first, and this ayah removes that option by requiring notice. The reason offered is not prudence but a statement about what God does not love, which applies regardless of who began it. That places a limit on conduct which survives the other side's misconduct entirely.

crossReferences.why: Describes the established treaty-breaking that this rule of notice is set against.
Uses the same verb for throwing something behind the back, there of scripture rather than a treaty.
Insists on the same distinction, that an agreement being kept must be honoured to its term.

studies.applyIt: If you have decided that an arrangement with someone is over, say so before you act on it. Most of the damage people do to each other happens in the gap between one person deciding and the other finding out. This ayah closes that gap, and it closes it on the side that would have benefited from leaving it open.

studies.title: What You Spend Comes Back
studies.meaning: An instruction about preparation whose stated aim is deterrence rather than use. The verb names making an opponent wary, so what is being organised is a discouragement rather than an attack. The list then opens outwards to a group nobody can identify, which commentators read as an admission of the limits of human intelligence placed inside a practical instruction. The ayah closes on money: whatever is spent in God's way is returned in full, and nobody is short-changed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the passages on treaties and during a period of continuing conflict. The community had almost no cavalry and had gone into the earlier engagement with a handful of horses between them. The commentators read the phrase about others unknown as covering parties whose hostility had not yet shown itself, and note that the instruction concerns capability rather than any named opponent.

keyTerms.note: The verb for getting something ready in advance, related to the word for counting. It carries the sense of a thing counted out and set aside beforehand, not improvised at the moment of need.
From the same root used earlier in this surah for something bound over the hearts of the men. Horses kept tied and fed at readiness were an expense borne in peacetime, which is what the word names.
A causative from the root for awe. What is asked for is an effect on the other party's calculation, which is why the ayah states a purpose rather than any use for what has been prepared.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A horse was the most expensive thing a household in Medina could keep. It ate grain rather than grazing, needed water every day, and produced nothing at all in ordinary times. Keeping one tied and fed was a standing cost with no return unless it was needed. That is why the ayah moves straight from horses to spending, and closes with a promise of repayment.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for tethering here comes from the same root the surah used earlier for something bound over the hearts of the men before the battle. The image is one rope: an animal held ready at a post, and a person held together under pressure. Arabic lets both senses live inside a single set of three letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is aimed at preventing a fight rather than at winning one, and the ayah says so in its own words. That reframing matters for how the whole passage reads. It also admits, inside the instruction itself, that those receiving it cannot see the full picture, since there are others they do not know. Preparation is therefore asked for as a discipline rather than as a response to a visible threat.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction that follows immediately if the other side inclines towards peace.
States the same promise about what is spent in God's way, with an image for the return.
Repeats the guarantee about spending in the plainest possible form, outside any conflict.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you maintain that you hope never to use: a savings buffer, a first aid kit, a skill you keep current, a friendship kept warm with someone you rarely need. Add one item to that list this month. The whole logic of this ayah is that readiness is worth paying for precisely while nothing is happening.

studies.title: If They Incline To Peace
studies.meaning: An instruction whose grammar mirrors itself: they lean, so you lean. The same verb serves both sides, which makes the response an answer rather than a concession. Then the obvious objection is raised and met in advance, since inclining towards peace is exactly what a deceiver would exploit. The reply offers no way of detecting deception. It names a sufficiency instead, and then points backwards at help that had already arrived through two channels, one unseen and one entirely human.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the ayah about preparation, which is what makes the ordering worth noticing: readiness first, then an instruction to accept peace if it is offered. The commentators discuss whether this ayah stands alongside the surah's other instructions and record differing views. The support named at the end refers back to the encounter this surah has been recounting throughout.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a wing. The verb describes a bird tilting to change direction, so inclining towards peace is pictured as a turn already begun rather than a position already reached.
From the root for wholeness and safety that also gives the words for submission and for the greeting. Peace in Arabic is named as an intact condition rather than as the absence of fighting.
From the verb to count or reckon. It says that when the sum is done this single item covers the total, which is why the Quran uses the word for confidence rather than for comfort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Truces in Arabia were sought and broken constantly, and a party accepting one took a real risk, since the interval could be used to prepare. Everyone understood that, and everyone accepted truces anyway, because the alternative was permanent war between people who shared wells and roads. This instruction sits inside a world that already knew both halves of the problem.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that God is enough for you occurs twice in the Quran, at 8:62 and again two ayat later at 8:64, and nowhere else at all. The two are addressed to the same person and separated only by a sentence about hearts being brought together, and the second adds the believers alongside God in the same breath.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage handles a real dilemma without pretending it away. Accepting an offer of peace exposes you, and the ayah neither denies that nor promises the offer is sincere. What it does is change what the exposure is measured against. And the reminder that follows is careful: help had come both from God and through people, so reliance is not being set in opposition to ordinary human support.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction on preparation that this passage immediately qualifies.
States the same principle as a limit, that an offer of peace closes the permission to fight.
Addresses the other side of the question, when an offer would come from weakness.

studies.applyIt: If someone has made a small move towards repairing something with you, and you suspect it is not entirely sincere, answer it anyway. Match the size of their move and no more. The ayah does not ask you to be naive or to drop your own preparation. It asks you not to be the one who refuses to lean back.

studies.title: What Money Could Not Buy
studies.meaning: A claim about a limit. The joining of hearts is named, and then the passage states exactly what could not have achieved it: everything on earth, spent. That is an unusual way to make a point, since it concedes the enormous power of the resource before denying it this one result. Commentators connect the statement to the particular hostility between groups in Medina before the emigration, kept alive across generations and resistant to every arrangement tried on it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The two main tribal groups of the city had fought a long series of wars, the last of them shortly before the emigration, and the enmity ran through families and alliances. Add to that emigrants arriving from Mecca with nothing and needing to be housed, and the community described here was assembled out of parties with genuine grievances. The commentators read the ayah against exactly that background.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to grow accustomed to something. What it names is not agreement but familiarity: hearts brought into the habit of one another. The same three letters give the word for a thousand.

A conditional marked as contrary to fact and addressed to one person. Naming the largest imaginable sum and then denying it the result is a way of measuring the thing achieved, not of criticising money.
From the verb to count. The phrase occurs twice in this surah and nowhere else in the Quran, and this second time it adds the believers alongside, so sufficiency is named as including people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reconciliation between feuding clans in Arabia was bought. Blood money was paid, marriages arranged, hostages exchanged, and a wealthy mediator could sometimes end a feud by covering both sides' debts out of his own property. It was a recognised and expensive undertaking. The ayah speaks to people who knew precisely what such a settlement cost and how long it usually lasted.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for joining hearts appears in this exact form only in this ayah. A closely related form occurs at 3:103, where the same act is described for the same community with a different pronoun attached. Both passages concern the city of Medina, and neither treats the reconciliation as the natural outcome of anything that happened there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah identifies something that resources cannot produce and names it precisely: not cooperation, which money buys constantly, but the familiarity of hearts with each other. That distinction is worth holding onto. It also implies that a community's cohesion is not an achievement its members can claim, which changes how they ought to hold it: as something received, and therefore as something that could be withdrawn.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same joining of hearts for the same community, in almost identical words.
Names the dispute that undoes what this ayah describes, and what it costs a group.
Shows what the joined hearts looked like in practice, between those same two groups.

studies.applyIt: Think of a friendship or a family bond that survived something it should not have. Try to account for it. You will find that you cannot, entirely. Say thank you for it this week, to God and then to the person, in whatever words you actually use. The ayah's point is that this one was never yours to arrange.

studies.title: Twenty Against Two Hundred
studies.meaning: A ratio is given and the quality producing it is named, and it is not skill or equipment. Twenty steadfast against two hundred, a hundred against a thousand. The reason offered at the end concerns the other side rather than the believers, and it is not a claim about their courage. They are described as people who do not grasp things, which commentators explain as fighting without knowing what it is for. The passage is then revised two ayat later.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the period when the community was organising for continued conflict. The commentators treat this ayah as the earlier of a pair and the one immediately following as its revision, and they discuss the relationship between them at length. The ratio given here is halved in the next ayah with a reason attached to the change, and both stand in the text in that order.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for stirring somebody to act, from a root also connected with wearing away through longing. It names persuasion rather than command, which suits an instruction given to one man about many.
The active participle of the verb for patience. It names people by a settled quality rather than by a passing state, so what produces the ratio is character rather than a feeling on the day.

A verb for understanding something below its surface, distinct from simply knowing it. What is denied to the other side is comprehension of what they are doing, which commentators read as why their numbers do not hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A fighting force in Arabia was a coalition, and coalitions came apart. Men fought for their clan's honour and left when the honour was satisfied or the risk grew, so a larger force was frequently a looser one. Understanding what a fight was actually for held people in place longer than numbers ever did. The ratio here would have sounded extraordinary but not absurd.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one immediately after it give two different ratios for the same situation, one to ten and then one to two, with the second explicitly described as a lightening. The Quran keeps both in the text in sequence rather than replacing one with the other, and the pair is one of the standard examples in the classical study of how instructions develop.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates strength in a quality rather than in a resource, and then names the opposing weakness as a failure of understanding rather than of nerve. Together those make a claim about what actually holds people in a hard place, which is knowing what it is for. The claim reaches well beyond a battlefield, and it is why the concession that follows concerns weakness rather than numbers.

crossReferences.why: Revises this ratio in the very next ayah, and gives the reason for the change.
Reports the same disproportion in an earlier account, with the same explanation from the smaller side.
Names the same two things asked for here, standing firm and remembering, a few ayat earlier.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the strength named here is endurance rather than talent. Pick the thing you are worst at sticking with and cut it down until you can hold it every day for a month. Ten minutes, not an hour. The ratio in this ayah is produced by people who do not stop, and nothing else about them is mentioned at all.

studies.title: God Knows There Is Weakness
studies.meaning: An adjustment announced openly, with its reason given plainly. The word placed first means now, marking a change of terms, and what follows halves the ratio set two ayat earlier. Then comes the explanation: He knows there is weakness in you. Nothing is concealed and nobody is blamed. Commentators note that the ayah both makes the standard easier and states why, so the concession is recorded permanently rather than quietly applied and forgotten.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the previous ayah and revising it. The classical sources report that the earlier ratio was found hard by the community and that this ayah came in response. The commentators discuss the pair at length as an example of instructions being adjusted, and preserve both. The word for weakness is read as covering numbers, equipment and resolve together.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for the present moment, placed first for emphasis. Its presence marks a change of terms explicitly, which is unusual: the text states that what applies now differs from what applied before.
The verb for reducing a weight or making a load easier to carry. It treats the earlier instruction as something borne rather than as a rule kept, which is why the reduction is described physically.

The plain noun, with no qualification and no apology attached to it. Commentators read it as covering numbers, equipment and resolve, and note that it is stated as knowledge rather than as an accusation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The community's material position had not improved quickly. Horses were few, armour was scarce, and many of the men were working to feed households in a city that was not their own. Weakness in that setting was a description rather than a failing. Being told that the requirement had been reduced because the shortfall was known would have landed as relief and not as reproach.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for lightening a load here is the same one used at 4:28, in the sentence saying that God wishes to lighten things for you, since the human being was created weak. The two ayat share both words, the lightening and the weakness, and they are among the few places where a reduction in what is asked appears with its reason attached.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a concession on the record with its reason beside it, which is a particular kind of honesty. It would have been simpler to state the lower figure alone. Instead the earlier one stands, the change is announced, and the weakness is named as already known rather than newly discovered. That treats a community's actual capacity as a legitimate input rather than as something exhortation should override.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier ratio that this ayah revises, two lines before it in the same passage.
Uses the same two words, lightening and weakness, in a sentence about what is asked of people.
States the general principle that nothing is required of a soul beyond its capacity.

studies.applyIt: Look at a commitment you made to yourself and have quietly failed at for months. Instead of renewing it, halve it. Write the smaller version down and say plainly why: there is weakness in you, and pretending otherwise has not worked. This ayah does exactly that, in public, and nothing about it is treated as shameful.

studies.title: You Wanted What Was Passing
studies.meaning: A correction delivered to a whole community, phrased first as a general statement about a prophet's position and then as direct address. Two desires are set opposite each other in a single line: the goods of this world, and the Hereafter. The commentators connect the passage to a decision taken after the battle and record the consultation that preceded it. What the ayah names is the motive rather than the decision, which is why the lines after it turn to forgiveness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, directly after the encounter at Badr, where a number of the opposing force were taken alive. The classical sources report a consultation about what should be done and record differing counsel given at it. This ayah and the two after it belong to that episode, and the commentators discuss them together. The reports agree on the outline and differ over who advised what.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to bind, since a captive's hands were tied. Arabic names the person by the physical fact of restraint rather than by any legal standing, which is how the Quran uses the word throughout.
From a root meaning thickness or density. The verb carries the sense of making something solid, so what it names is a position firmly established rather than a single engagement won.

keyTerms.gloss: the passing goods of this world
keyTerms.note: The first word comes from a root meaning what appears from the side and does not last, the opposite of what is substantial. The phrase occurs in this exact form only here, and it carries its own judgement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransoming captives was ordinary Arabian practice and a recognised source of income. Families paid to recover their men, with the amount depending on standing, and both sides expected the arrangement. Nobody involved would have thought of it as anything other than normal. That is what makes the correction here striking: a routine practice is named as a desire rather than treated as a procedure.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the goods of this world occurs in this exact form only in this ayah. Its first word comes from a root meaning something that shows itself from the side and passes on, which Arabic uses for a thing glimpsed rather than held. The word carries the argument before the sentence makes it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not call the decision a sin and does not undo it. What it does is name a motive that had gone unexamined and set it beside another. That is a distinctive kind of correction: nobody is told they broke a rule, and everybody is shown what they were actually reaching for. The ayat that follow then place the whole episode explicitly under forgiveness.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately, placing the same episode under a decree and then under permission.
Turns to the captives themselves, offering them something better than what was taken.
Names the same two possibilities for captives, in a later passage on the same subject.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you made recently that was defensible in every way, and ask what you actually wanted from it. Not whether it was right. What you wanted. Most of us never separate those two questions, and this passage separates them without ever concluding that the decision itself was wrong.

studies.title: A Decree That Went Before
studies.meaning: Two ayat that move in opposite directions and belong together. The first names a punishment that did not happen and attributes its absence to something written beforehand, which commentators explain in more than one way. The second then permits what was taken, describing it with two words for what is wholesome. Read together the pair says that something was seriously wrong and that it is entirely settled, and it says both without hedging either half.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the passage about the aftermath of Badr. The commentators differ over what the prior decree refers to, some reading it as the general principle that no community is punished before an instruction has reached it, others as something specific to that occasion. The reports about the episode itself are numerous and vary in detail, and the classical commentaries set the readings out side by side.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for something written. Used of a decision it names a matter already fixed, and the verb after it says the writing came first, which is what removes the punishment.
The verb for getting somewhere ahead of somebody, used in racing. Applied to a decree it places the decision earlier than the event, so the outcome was settled before the choice was made.
Two words that recur together across the Quran. The first concerns permission and the second concerns quality, and pairing them says a thing is both allowed and good rather than merely tolerated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food and wealth acquired in doubtful circumstances were a live worry in a society without records. A man might inherit from a relative whose dealings were unclear, or receive a share of something whose origin nobody could trace. Being told plainly that something was clean to use answered a real and constant anxiety, which is why the second ayah speaks of eating rather than of owning.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words paired here for what is lawful and wholesome occur together four times in the Quran, and every one of those four sits inside an instruction about eating rather than about owning. The question of clean and unclean gain is addressed through the most ordinary act available, which puts an abstract matter in a person's hands several times a day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pair holds together two things people usually keep apart: a serious fault and a complete settlement. Nothing is minimised in the first ayah and nothing is withheld in the second. That combination is characteristic of how the Quran handles the community's own mistakes, and it is more demanding than either half alone, since a reader has to accept the seriousness and the clearance at once.

crossReferences.why: Names the desire behind the episode that these two ayat then place under forgiveness.
States one of the readings commentators give for the prior decree named here.
Uses the same pair of words for what is lawful and wholesome, in an instruction about eating.

studies.applyIt: Notice how rarely you allow both halves of this at once with yourself. Either the fault was not serious, or it is not really settled. Pick one thing you have already made right and stop reopening it. Say the second sentence to yourself as plainly as the first: that was wrong, and it is finished.

studies.title: Better Than What Was Taken
studies.meaning: An instruction to speak to prisoners, and what is to be said is an offer rather than a warning. The condition named is inward, any good in the heart, and what is promised in return is more than what was lost, with forgiveness added on top. The second ayah then handles the obvious risk by pointing backwards: an earlier betrayal has already happened and its outcome is visible in the present situation. Neither ayah threatens anything.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the ransom arrangements following Badr. The commentators report that some of those taken had been ransomed by their families at considerable cost, and that this ayah addresses them directly through the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Several report that a number of them later joined the community. The address is unusual for being aimed at people held by the community rather than at the community itself.
