keyTerms.note: The same word used three ayat earlier, but the address has changed completely. There it names a category under discussion; here it names a group being spoken to, through an intermediary who is told what to say.
The plain verb for giving, with the recipients addressed directly as you. Nothing in the sentence depends on their release or on any action of theirs; the condition named is entirely inward.
From the root for a place or position. The verb means putting somebody in a position with respect to another, so the claim concerns how the present situation came about rather than anything owed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ransomed captive went home poorer and diminished. Families sold property to raise the sum, and a man who had cost his relatives a herd carried that fact for years afterwards. The promise here of something better than what was taken speaks directly to a specific and humiliating loss, in a society where such a debt was remembered publicly and repeated often.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran contains very few instructions to address a particular group of prisoners, and this is one of them. What is to be said to them contains no condition about their conduct at all, only about what is in their hearts, and it promises them more than what was taken rather than the return of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The offer is made to people who had just fought against the community, and it is made while they are still being held. The timing is the striking part, since no change in circumstances is required before it. The condition is also located entirely inside them, in a place nobody else can inspect, which means the community is told to hold out an offer whose acceptance it can never verify.

crossReferences.why: Describes the decision that left these people in the community's hands, three ayat earlier.
Names the captive among those to be fed, in a passage about ordinary generosity.
Holds out the same possibility of a changed relation with people currently on the other side.

studies.applyIt: Say the generous thing to someone before their situation improves, not after. Most of us wait until a person has changed before offering them anything, which means the offer arrives once it is no longer needed. Find one person this week who is still in the wrong, and say the encouraging sentence to them anyway.

studies.title: Allies Of One Another
studies.meaning: A relation is defined by naming who holds it. Two groups are described by what they did, one having believed and emigrated and struggled with property and person, the other having given shelter and given help, and then they are declared allies of each other. A third group is named next, believers who did not emigrate, and the relation is withheld. Then an exception cuts across everything: a call for help must be answered, except against a people with whom there is a treaty.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the closing section of the surah, which sets out the arrangement between the emigrants and the people of Medina. The commentators read the passage as describing the specific structure of that community rather than a permanent arrangement, and note that the surah's final ayah adjusts it. The classical discussion of how far it applied afterwards is long, and the views differ.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cut off or abandon. The word names leaving by severing rather than by travelling, which is why it is used of the departure from Mecca and not of any ordinary journey.
The verb for taking somebody into your house. The same root was used earlier in the surah of God giving refuge to the community, so what people did and what God did are named by one word.
From a root meaning nearness. The word covers the whole bundle of obligations between allies, and Arabic uses the same root for a friend, a patron, a client and a guardian.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arriving in a city with no kin meant arriving with no standing whatsoever. The arrangement described here paired incoming households with local ones, and the pairing carried real obligations: housing, work, and the duty to answer if someone was attacked. It replaced a system based on descent with one based on shared commitment, in a society where descent had previously decided everything.
studies.didYouKnow: The two acts named for the people of Medina in this ayah, giving shelter and giving help, are the same two verbs used at 8:26 for what God did for the community when it was small and frightened. The surah uses one pair of words for both, fifty ayat apart, and never pauses to explain the connection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage builds a community out of actions rather than out of birth, and it says so by listing verbs. What binds people is what they did, which means the bond can be entered and, by implication, can lapse. The exception about existing treaties is also worth noticing: an obligation to fellow believers is limited by an agreement already given to others, which places a promise above a preference.

crossReferences.why: Completes the same structure, adding those who came later and the claims of kinship.
Uses the same two verbs for shelter and help, applied there to what God did for the community.
Describes the same two groups in the same terms, and reports what the arrangement looked like.

studies.applyIt: Notice who would actually answer if you called at two in the morning, and who you would answer for. The list is usually shorter than the list of people you like. Add one name to it deliberately this year, and tell them. The alliance in this ayah is made of things done, not of things felt.

studies.title: Unless You Do This
studies.meaning: A short ayah carrying a large conditional. The first clause states a fact about the other side, using the same word for alliance just applied to the believers. The second names the consequence of not doing something, and what that something is has to be supplied from the ayah before it. Commentators read it as the mutual support just described, and note that what is threatened is disorder in general rather than the defeat of any one party.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately following the description of the arrangement between the emigrants and the people of Medina. The commentators read this ayah as completing that passage rather than opening a new subject, and connect the warning to the practical position of a small community whose members were spread across a region and depended on knowing exactly who would answer for whom.

keyTerms.note: The same word used in the preceding ayah of the believers. Applying it identically to both sides describes a structure rather than delivering a verdict, since alliance is something both groups have.

The word carries three different senses in this surah: a test, persecution, and now general disorder. Its root sense of assaying metal in fire lies under all three, and context decides which is meant.

From the verb for something going bad, used of food and of water. It names decay rather than crime, so what is threatened is a society losing its soundness rather than committing a particular offence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a person without a clear alliance was a danger to everybody, including themselves. Nobody knew who would answer for them, which meant nobody knew what an injury to them would cost. Ambiguity of that kind produced feuds, since a wrong with no known price was settled by whoever felt strongest at the time. Clear lines were a form of public safety.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for turmoil appears four times in this surah and carries a different weight almost every time: a trial that does not fall only on the guilty at 8:25, wealth and children as a test at 8:28, persecution at 8:39, and general disorder here. Few Quranic words shift their sense so much inside one surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah gives a reason for social arrangements that is not about advantage. What is at stake in people knowing where they stand is described as the health of a place rather than the position of a group. That treats clarity of obligation as a public good in itself, and it explains why the surah spends its closing ayat on the question of who owes what to whom.

crossReferences.why: Describes the arrangement whose absence this ayah warns about, in the line immediately before.
Names the same danger of general corruption and gives the same kind of structural answer.
Restates the same relation of mutual alliance in a later surah, with the duties listed out.

studies.applyIt: Look at one arrangement in your life where nobody has said out loud who is responsible for what: a shared household task, a family obligation, a piece of work between two teams. Ambiguity there is not neutral; it quietly generates resentment. Say the sentence that fixes it this week, even if it costs you the easier half.

studies.title: The Believers In Truth
studies.meaning: A verdict repeated from the surah's opening, with a completely different description standing behind it. At the start the same sentence followed prayer and spending; here it follows emigration, struggle, and the giving of shelter. Both times the identical pair of things is promised afterwards. The effect of the repetition is to say that these are one category rather than two levels, and that the quiet practices and the costly ones arrive at the same standing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the end of the surah, summarising the arrangement described in the preceding ayat. The commentators note the deliberate echo of the surah's fourth ayah and read the two as bracketing everything between them. The description here belongs to a community that had by then been through emigration, a battle and a long stretch of pressure, and the ayah names those as its content.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning effort carried to the point of exhaustion. The word names the spending of capacity rather than any particular action, and the earlier ayah specifies property and person as the two things spent.

An intensifier placed after the noun, working like a seal pressed onto a document. The same construction closes the surah's opening description, so the two occurrences frame everything that lies between.
The adjective means noble or open-handed rather than large. It describes the manner of the giving rather than the quantity given, which is how Arabic praises a host rather than a harvest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two groups named had made opposite kinds of sacrifice. One left everything behind and arrived with nothing; the other kept its houses and divided them. Neither is ranked above the other here. In a society where the giver and the receiver held fixed and unequal positions, describing both with a single verdict was a substantial rearrangement of how standing actually worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence naming these the believers in truth occurs exactly twice in the Quran, at 8:4 and here at 8:74, and the same promise of forgiveness and generous provision follows both. Seventy ayat separate them, and the whole account of the battle lies in between, so the surah opens and closes on one identical verdict.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repeating a verdict with a different basis says something neither description could say on its own: that what makes the label true is not one specific act. Prayer and spending in one place, emigration and shelter in the other, and the same seal on both. That protects a reader who will never be asked for the second kind of thing, and it keeps the first kind from being treated as a lesser version.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same verdict at the surah's opening, with prayer and spending as its basis.
Describes the same two groups and the relation established between them.
Names the same two groups together, and adds those who follow them afterwards.

studies.applyIt: You are probably measuring your faith against a story of someone who gave up much more than you have. Stop for a moment and read the surah's other description, the one at its opening: prayer kept up, and something given from what you have. Do those two well this week and let that be the whole of the assessment.

studies.title: Nearer By Kinship
studies.meaning: The surah closes by opening its arrangement and then qualifying it. Those who came later are declared to belong, with no lesser status attached, which commentators read as deliberately closing off a distinction that could otherwise have hardened. Then a second clause adds something the preceding ayat had not: those related by blood have a nearer claim on one another. Commentators read this as bearing chiefly on inheritance, and note that it restores kinship without restoring the whole older system.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the final ayah of the surah. The commentators report that in the earliest period in Medina the pairing between emigrants and helpers carried a claim on inheritance, and they read this closing clause as adjusting that. The reports differ in their details. What is agreed is that the surah ends by placing kinship back inside the structure it has just built, without cancelling anything else in it.

keyTerms.note: The phrase is left without a stated point of reference, so it simply means later than what has been described. That vagueness makes the door it opens permanent rather than tied to any particular year.
The second word is the plural of the word for a womb. Arabic names blood relation by the organ, so kinship is expressed as shared origin in a body rather than as a line of descent traced on paper.

The phrase can name the revealed text or a decree written beforehand, and commentators take it both ways here. Either reading places the claim of kinship outside human arrangement and beyond local custom.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance was the sharpest question in any Arabian household, because property held a family's position and no court existed to appeal to. The pairing of emigrants with helpers had been generous enough to include it, which meant a man might inherit from someone he had known two years rather than from a brother. Workable in an emergency, and hard to sustain beyond one.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about those of kinship being nearer to one another occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 33:6, in almost identical words. Both appear at a point where a community's structure is being set out, and both add the claim of blood relation as a qualification to an arrangement that had been built on something else entirely.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah's last sentence adds kinship back after several ayat that built a community out of choices. That is a careful ending. It says that a community formed by commitment does not abolish the ties people were born into, and that both hold at the same time. Placing the claim in the Book of God rather than in custom also means it is not simply the old order returning on its own authority.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the arrangement based on emigration and shelter that this ayah then qualifies.
Repeats the same clause about kinship in almost identical words, in a similar context.
States the claim of relatives on what is left behind, in the surah that sets out the shares.

studies.applyIt: There is a relative you have let drift because the friendship never quite worked. The surah's last line does not ask you to like them. It puts them nearer than the arrangement you would have chosen. Send one message this week that acknowledges the connection without pretending it is something warmer than it is.
